summary.text: Specialize to \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and choose an arbitrarily large prime \(p\). The only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)\le2\), whereas \(p>e^4\) implies \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(\operatorname{PF}(m)\) denotes the set of prime factors of \(m\), then
\[
a(n)=\#\{k:1\le k\le n,\ \operatorname{PF}(k)\subseteq \operatorname{PF}(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
Here the power is the usual real power, and the natural numbers on the right are regarded as real numbers when compared with the left-hand side.

The key observation is that \(a(n)\) stays bounded along the primes. More precisely, if \(p\) is prime, then
\[
a(p)\le 2.
\]
Indeed, the only positive divisors relevant to the argument are as follows. Suppose \(1\le k\le p\) and every prime factor of \(k\) divides \(p\). If \(k=1\), then \(k\) is one of the two possible values. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). By the defining condition on \(k\), this prime \(q\) divides \(p\). Since \(p\) itself is prime, its only prime divisor is \(p\), so \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Because \(k>0\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while the assumed range gives \(k\le p\). Hence \(k=p\). Therefore every integer counted by \(a(p)\) lies in \(\{1,p\}\), proving \(a(p)\le2\). In fact both \(1\) and \(p\) qualify, so \(a(p)=2\), although only the upper bound is needed.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the proposed lower bound were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a natural number \(M\) satisfying
\[
M>e^4.
\]
Such an \(M\) exists by the Archimedean property. Next choose a prime \(p\) with
\[
p\ge \max\{N,M\}.
\]
The existence of such a prime is the standard fact that primes are unbounded. For completeness, this can be seen directly: given any natural bound \(B\), the integer \((B+1)!+1\) is greater than \(1\), so it has a prime divisor \(p\). If \(p\le B+1\), then \(p\) divides \((B+1)!\) as well as \((B+1)!+1\), and hence would divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible. Thus \(p>B+1>B\). Applying this to a bound at least \(\max\{N,M\}\) supplies the required prime.

Since \(p\ge M>e^4\), and the natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers,
\[
\log p>\log(e^4)=4.
\]
Both sides are positive, so taking positive square roots preserves the strict inequality. Consequently,
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>4^{1/2}=2.
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge N\), so the assumed eventual lower bound, evaluated at \(n=p\), gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
The prime-input estimate gives \(a(p)\le2\). Combining these inequalities yields
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)\le2,
\]
an impossibility.

Therefore the claimed statement is false: for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold \(N\) can make \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) hold for every \(n\ge N\). Indeed, the inequality fails at every sufficiently large prime, because \(a(p)=2\) whereas \(\sqrt{\log p}\) is unbounded along the primes.
